 INTERACTIVE: Selangor among seven states with higher flood losses involving homes
 By YUEN MEIKENG 
 Wednesday, 18 Nov 2026
 | 7:00 AM MYT
 share 
 bookmark 
 PETALING JAYA: Seven states recorded higher losses from flood damage to homes, despite an overall decline in Malaysia’s flood-related losses.
 Selangor saw the third highest jump in flood losses involving living quarters - the costs more than doubled from RM6.63mil in 2024 to RM15.29mil last year.
 The top two states with the biggest spike were Sarawak and Sabah.
 The value of losses in Sarawak surged by RM30.35mil - from RM2.2mil in 2024 to RM32.55mil last year, based on data from the Department of Statistics Malaysia.
 Sabah’s flood losses involving residential properties rose from RM17.32mil to RM27.71mil in the same period.
 This goes against the nationwide trend, as Malaysia’s overall flood-related losses - including damage to homes, vehicles, business premises, industries and public infrastructure - dropped from RM933.4mil in 2024 to RM636.9mil last year.
 The other four states with higher losses for living quarters were Pahang, Johor, Perlis and Perak.
 The trend for each state can be seen in the graph below:
 On the reasons for higher flood losses in some states, experts said it was mainly to do with urbanisation and the terrain of the affected areas.
 “As Malaysia becomes more developed and urbanised, the amount and cost of assets exposed to flood damage will increase.
 “Flooding in the padi fields of Kedah will be less costly than flooding in Kuala Lumpur,” said Universiti Malaya (UM) meteorologist Prof Datuk Dr Azizan Abu Samah.
 Most of the urbanised areas in Klang Valley and Sarawak are also on low-lying flood plains of rivers, making them flood-prone, he added.
 UM meteorologist Associate Professor Dr Sheeba Chenoli said the increase in flood losses involving homes does not necessarily mean flooding has become more severe, but it is due to a combination of many factors.
 “Our study in 2025 showed that some stations recorded increases in extreme rainfall while others showed decreases too,” she said.
 Sheeba said Selangor is mostly an urbanised area, where there are concrete and asphalt that cut rainwater absorption, as well as drains that are often built for older rainfall patterns.
 “Low-lying and reclaimed land, and housing built near river floodplains can also add to the spike in losses.
 “The monsoon flash floods in dense areas hit many homes at once. Blocked drains and tidal effects at the coast make it worse,” said Sheeba, who is with the university’s geography department.
 For Sabah and Sarawak, it is more about geography and exposure.
 “Large river basins, flat floodplains and heavy monsoon rainfall mean rivers overflow slowly and widely.
 “Many settlements in these states sit by rivers, and rural homes are often less flood-proofed.
 “Land clearing upstream can also speed up runoff.
 “The most affected districts were Bintulu, Serian and Selangau in Sarawak, and Keningau and Beaufort in Sabah,” said Sheeba.
 On the flip side, there were also states which saw a drop in flood losses involving homes from 2024 to 2025, according to the data.
 The three states with the sharpest dips were Kelantan, Terengganu and Kedah.
 Check out the graph below to see which states saw increases or decreases in flood losses to homes.
 Such data is according to the department’s series of special reports on the impact of floods in Malaysia.
 Between 2022 and 2025, Malaysia recorded a total of RM3.35bil in overall flood losses from living quarters, vehicles, business premises, industries like manufacturing and agriculture as well as public infrastructure.
 Within this period, Kelantan topped the list with the highest total value of damage from the floods.
 The state, located in the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia, sustained a total of RM685.2mil in flood losses, followed by Terengganu with RM588.9mil and Johor with RM445.2mil.
 At the district level, Batu Pahat in Johor recorded the highest total value of flood damage to homes from 2022 to 2025.
 It recorded a total of RM90.55mil in losses, followed by Pasir Mas in Kelantan with RM88.39mil and Besut in Terengganu with RM51.74mil.
 Here’s a more detailed look the flood losses in other districts:
 Prof Azizan said there are two types of floods that can cause damage and losses - flash floods and major floods.
 “Flash floods are due to a single thunderstorm event with a very high rainfall intensity, for example, at 100mm in one hour.
 “This challenges the drainage around the area, or how fast water can be channeled away,” Prof Azizan said, describing it as an urban issue.
 To overcome it, he said the authorities should look into the design and capacity of the drainage system and flood storage near the hotspot.
 “Since it is an urban phenomena, it can be a costly and damaging event due to the population density.
 “Assets such as cars, motorcycles and household furniture can be exposed to damage,” he said.
 Major flooding, he said, is when floods are due to continuous rainfall, such as from 48 to 72 hours over a large area.
 “Such events are the ones that can inundate about 70% of Kelantan or flooding over a big area.
 “The flooding is due to the river breaking its banks and spreading across areas,” he said.
 To minimise the impact of floods, Sheeba said greater attention must be given to climate change adaptation, or building resilience to hazards such as flooding, droughts and heatwaves.
 “This requires practical measures, including better evacuation and early warning systems, improved drainage networks, more retention ponds and nature-based solutions such as sponge cities (urban areas with green features that can prevent floods).
 “Rather than simply diverting excess rainwater away, sponge cities aim to absorb, retain and gradually release water through ecological infrastructure such as wetlands, green spaces, permeable surfaces and vegetation,” she added.
 With the Northeast Monsoon season to last until March next year, Malaysia can expect between three and five episodes of continuous heavy rain during the initial phase, from November to January.
